newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Remote Tokelau gets first telephones.
newsitem.headline: Remote Tokelau gets first telephones.

text.p: Residents of the Tokelau Islands in the Pacific were holding festivities on Friday to celebrate the arrival of telephones, a government official said.
Government-owned TeleTok, or Tokelau Telecommunications Corporation, was opened this week and started operations on Friday via a digital network.

Logotasi Iosefa, a spokesman for the Tokelau Apia Liaison Office in Western Samoa, told Reuters it would be the first time the 1,600 people of Tokelau did not have to gather on one of the islands' three atolls to celebrate a national event.

"What they're doing is having conference facilities on the phone, and so the leaders and the people of one atoll will be able to speak to their colleagues and families on the next one," Iosefa said. Festivities would include dancing and feasting.
Until now, islanders wanting to communicate with each other had to use high frequency radios situated in small central rooms in the villages.

"That is perhaps not totally adequate for the present times. It is not very private, so the advent of a new system will mean that people who choose to have a phone in their own home will be able to make a confidential and private telephone conversation," Iosefa said.
"This is a very new innovation for Tokelau."
He estimated there were around 200 households on the islands, and said most would want a telephone.
Only local calls would be possible initially, but it was hoped that by mid-April the people of Tokelau would be able to make and receive international phone and fax calls.

Tokelau, a territory without airports or harbours, is 480 km (300 miles) north of Western Samoa. The three atolls cover a land area of just 12 square km (4.6 square miles) and the people make a living from fishing and copra.

New Zealand delegated its administrative responsibility for the atolls to local institutions in 1992 but, because of Tokelau's isolation and lack of resources, retains the authority to intervene in special circumstances.

Aliki Faipule Teao, Tokelau's Ulu or titular leader who is also the chairman of Teletok, said in a statement published by New Zealand's foreign ministry that the company would use any operating surpluses to reduce prices rather than maximising returns.
"For centuries, Tokelau people have customarily shared their fishing catches with their villages. Sharing TeleTok's profits will retain these values," he said.
